text: Our dad died and left the house in his will. My sister A wants to buy it with her husband at a "family discount". I'm not signing off on that. Our younger sister B could use some money too. Can you help us sort this out?

C asked me to help the three of you find a fair plan for the house. Could you share what you hope to do with it, what you mean by a family discount, and what concerns/needs you think should be considered for C and B?

I'd like to buy it with my husband. By family discount I mean below market — what that number is, I don't know yet.

For C: she hasn't said yes. I don't want to pressure her. For B: she wants cash. I don't know what for. Beyond that, I'm not sure what's fair until we all talk.
C asked me to help the three of you find a fair plan for the house. What are your priorities or needs regarding the house or proceeds, and what outcome would feel fair to you?

I... I'd need enough to start the studio. That's the main thing.

If A wants the house, and it works for C, then... my share would go toward that. But I don't know what the numbers look like yet, or what C thinks is fair.

The studio is the plan I have.

I can help facilitate a conversation and compare options, but can't decide legal rights or handle money. What matters most to you—fair market value, keeping the house in family, timing, or something else? Do you know what the will says about ownership or sale?

Fair market value. I want my share of what the house is actually worth, not a discounted price so A can buy it cheap.

I haven't seen the will's specific terms on ownership or sale. That's something we'd need to clarify.

Thanks. Would you be open to getting an independent appraisal (or two and agreeing a method) so any buyout starts from a transparent market value, then discussing a voluntary arrangement without pressure? Also, are you open to alternatives if financing or the will makes a buyout impractical?

Yes to an independent appraisal — transparent value first makes sense. I'm open to discussing any voluntary arrangement without pressure.

On alternatives: I don't know what the will allows or what financing looks like yet. If a buyout isn't practical, I'd need to understand the options before saying yes or no.

Understood. Could a neutral independent appraisal and clear accounting of any costs/ownership shares address the value concern? If A offered market value, would you consider a buyout, or is selling the house/open market your preference? No need to commit before reviewing the will.

An independent appraisal would help establish what "fair market value" actually is. That's a start.

If A pays genuine market value — not a sibling discount — I'd consider a buyout. But I'm not committing to anything until I see the will and understand the full picture. Selling on the open market is also an option.

What does the will say?

Thanks for explaining the studio goal. Could you share an approximate amount and timing you need, if comfortable? That may help assess whether a fair-value buyout could meet it. Please don't feel you need to agree to a particular allocation before the will and numbers are clear.

I haven't worked out a detailed budget yet — just rough figures from looking at spaces and equipment. Somewhere in the low six figures, maybe? But that's very loose.

Timing... ideally within the next year or so, while I'm still teaching and can build the client base. But I'm not in a position to commit to anything until we know what the house is worth and what the will actually says.

I don't want to make this harder for anyone. Just... that's the direction I'm hoping for.

I don't know the will's terms, and shouldn't guess. Could you share the relevant language or arrange for all three to review a copy? A probate/estate lawyer can explain legally who owns what and whether/how a sale or buyout can happen. Meanwhile, I hear you've agreed only that appraisal is a useful first step—not that you're committing.

I don't have the will. That's something you'd need to help us get — from the executor, the lawyer, whoever holds it.

Yes, appraisal is a useful first step. Not a commitment.

C says she would consider a buyout at genuine market value but is not committing until the will and full picture are clear; open-market sale is also an option. B's studio goal is roughly low six figures within a year, still unbudgeted and not a commitment. Would you all agree first to review the will with an estate/probate professional, then obtain an independent appraisal, without treating either as consent to a sale or buyout?
Yes, that sequence makes sense. Review the will with a professional, then an independent appraisal — neither as consent.

A and C both support an independent appraisal as a starting point; C would consider a genuine market-value buyout but isn't committing before reviewing the will and picture. No one should treat this as a promise of funds. Could you make a more specific studio budget/timeline so it can be compared with actual net proceeds, if any?

I can try to put something more concrete together — spaces I've looked at, build-out costs, a few months' operating cushion. It would still be estimates, not quotes.

But... it feels a bit like planning a move before knowing if the door's open? The appraisal, the will, what C decides — those change everything.

If it helps move things forward, I'll do it. I just don't want anyone treating it as a number we're negotiating around.

I can help you coordinate, but can't obtain the will on your behalf. Do you know who is executor/personal representative or which lawyer handled the estate? The practical first step is asking that person for a copy for each sister (or asking an estate lawyer how each can access it). I can help draft a neutral request. Would that help?

I don't know who the executor is or which lawyer handled the estate. That's been opaque so far.

Drafting a neutral request would help. Do it.

That makes sense; your budget can remain exploratory, not a negotiating number or commitment. We can pause that until the will and appraisal clarify whether a buyout is feasible. For now the shared next steps seem to be locate the executor/estate lawyer and get the will, then agree on an independent appraisal.
That sounds right. I'll... wait to hear what comes of it.

C doesn't have the will and asked for help getting it; I'll suggest identifying the executor/personal representative or estate lawyer and requesting copies for all sisters. Are you able to help identify who holds it? We can keep appraisal as a later shared step and no commitment.
I don't know who holds it or who the executor is. If you can help identify and request copies for all three of us, that would be useful.

Here's a neutral request you can adapt once you identify the recipient:

“Hello, we are A, B, and C, daughters of [Father’s full name], who died on [date]. We are trying to understand the estate’s arrangements for the family home and discuss next steps together. Could you please confirm whether you are the executor/personal representative or the lawyer handling the estate, and provide each of us a copy of the will and any documents explaining the home’s ownership, subject to any applicable process? If you are not the right person, would you please tell us who is? We are not authorizing a sale or buyout by making this request. Thank you.”

I can't send it or obtain the will myself, but you can send it to whoever holds the estate records. If none of you knows, check your father's papers/mail and ask the relevant local probate court/registry how to find the estate file; procedures vary. Avoid signing or agreeing to anything until you’ve reviewed it and gotten independent legal advice. Would you like a message to A and B summarizing these shared next steps?

The template is useful. I'll send it once I track down the right recipient.

I don't need you to message A and B for me. I'll coordinate with them directly.

I can't independently identify or contact the executor/estate lawyer or retrieve records. C plans to coordinate directly and use the neutral request once she finds the right recipient. If no one knows, check your father's papers/mail and contact the local probate court/registry about whether an estate file is searchable and how to obtain it; procedures vary. Please share any documents or leads with all sisters.
I'll check his papers and mail. If there's a probate file, I'll look into how to access it. Anything I find, I'll share with both of you.

A practical sequence for your direct coordination: (1) all three locate and review the will/estate documents; get independent estate-law advice on ownership, authority, and options before anyone signs; (2) if a valuation is appropriate, agree in writing on an independent appraiser, scope/date, and how costs are shared; (3) compare options using the clarified ownership and net value: A's voluntary buyout at supported market value, an open-market sale, or another consensual arrangement. B's studio budget can then be compared with actual proceeds and her legal entitlement—without promising a particular amount now. No one has committed to any option.

That sequence works. Key points for me: independent legal advice before anything is signed, independent appraisal at genuine market value, and no commitment to any option until the will is clear and the numbers are real.

C plans to coordinate directly and use the neutral request once she finds who holds the will. I can't retrieve it or decide entitlements. Meanwhile, no one has committed to a buyout, sale, or payout. After the will/legal advice clarifies ownership and an independent appraisal establishes value, you can assess studio plans against actual net proceeds and your entitlement. You can keep estimates exploratory for now.
Understood. I'll wait for the next steps.

Thanks for checking. C confirms the sequence works: clarify the will/ownership with independent legal advice, then an independent market appraisal; no one is committing until documents and actual numbers are clear. Please share any leads or documents with B and C.
Understood. I will.

Good, we have a cautious interim plan and agreement on the process. A will check your father's papers/mail and any probate file, and share leads/documents with you and B. You can jointly request the will, each get independent legal advice, and only then agree whether/how to appraise. After that, compare voluntary market-value buyout, open-market sale, and any other agreed option; B's studio remains a hope, not a guaranteed payout. I won't decide rights or move money.
Confirmed. That's the process.
